title: “My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?”
paragraphs:
“My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?”
The Cry That Shook Heaven, Broke Hell, and Opened the Door From Scandal to Grace
There are moments in life when pain becomes so overwhelming that words fail.
Moments when the prayers stop sounding polished.
Moments when faith feels more like survival than victory.
Moments when heaven seems silent.
You prayed.
You trusted.
You waited.
And still the marriage collapsed.
Still the diagnosis came.
Still the betrayal happened.
Still the grave closed over someone you loved.
Still the addiction returned.
Still the depression stayed.
And somewhere deep inside your soul, whether you dared say it aloud or not, a question formed:
“God... where are You?”
For many believers, those words feel dangerous.
Almost sinful.
Almost forbidden.
Yet one of the most powerful cries ever uttered in human history was not spoken by a doubter.
It was spoken by Jesus Christ Himself.
Hanging between heaven and earth.
Nails tearing through His flesh.
Blood streaming down the cross.
Darkness covering the land.
The sin of the world resting upon His shoulders.
And from His lips came these unforgettable words:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Matthew 27:46 records the moment:
"About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, 'Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?' that is, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?'"
The original Aramaic preserved by Matthew is:

אֵלִי אֵלִי לְמָא שְׁבַקְתַּנִי
(Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?)
Literally:
“My God, My God, for what purpose have You abandoned Me?”
Mark's Gospel preserves a slightly different Galilean pronunciation:

Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ λιμὰ σαβαχθανί
(Eloi, Eloi, lima sabachthani?)
This was not a random cry.
This was not a loss of faith.
This was not Jesus questioning whether God existed.
Something far deeper was happening.
To understand these words, we must travel back nearly one thousand years before Calvary.
To a shepherd king named David.
A man familiar with suffering.
A man acquainted with betrayal.
A man who wrote under divine inspiration:

אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
(Eli, Eli, lamah azavtani?)
Psalm 22:1
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”
The moment Jesus uttered those words from the cross, every Jewish listener would immediately recognize them.
Because Jesus was quoting Psalm 22.
And Psalm 22 is astonishing.
Written centuries before crucifixion was even practiced in Israel, it describes details that sound as if someone stood beneath the cross and recorded the events firsthand.
David wrote:
"All who see me mock me." (Psalm 22:7)
The crowds mocked Jesus.
David wrote:
"They pierce my hands and my feet." (Psalm 22:16)
Jesus' hands and feet were pierced.
David wrote:
"They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing." (Psalm 22:18)
Roman soldiers literally gambled for Christ's garments.
This was not coincidence.
This was prophecy.
When Jesus cried out Psalm 22:1, He was directing the world to the entire Psalm.
He was revealing that everything unfolding before their eyes had been written long before.
Yet there is an even deeper mystery.
Scripture teaches that Jesus was not merely suffering physical agony.
At that moment He was carrying something infinitely heavier.
The sins of humanity.
Your sins.
My sins.
Every lie.
Every act of lust.
Every betrayal.
Every act of violence.
Every secret thought.
Every hidden addiction.
Every scandal.
Every rebellion.
Every failure.
Isaiah 53:6 declares:
"The LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all."
The Hebrew word for iniquity is:

עָוֹן
(avon)
It refers not merely to wrongdoing but to guilt, corruption, and the consequences of sin.
All of it was placed upon Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
"God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God."
Think about that.
The only truly innocent human being who ever lived voluntarily stood in the place of the guilty.
The Holy One stood where the scandalous belonged.
The spotless Lamb stood where sinners deserved to stand.
The righteous absorbed the judgment of the unrighteous.
Why?
Because love demanded a substitute.
The holiness of God could not ignore sin.
The love of God refused to abandon sinners.
The cross is where perfect justice and perfect mercy embraced.
When Jesus cried,
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
He was experiencing the horror of bearing sin's judgment.
Not because the Father ceased loving the Son.
The Trinity was not broken.
The divine nature did not fracture.
But Christ, as humanity's substitute, was enduring the judgment that sin deserved.
He entered the darkness we created.
So we could enter the light He deserved.
He embraced abandonment.
So we could be adopted.
He carried condemnation.
So we could receive forgiveness.
He entered our scandal.
So we could receive His grace.
And perhaps this is why these words hit so deeply today.
Because many people reading this feel forsaken.
You feel forgotten.
You feel abandoned.
You feel unseen.
You feel like your mistakes have permanently disqualified you.
You smile in public while silently falling apart.
You attend church while carrying wounds nobody knows about.
You quote Scripture while privately questioning whether God still wants you.
You wonder if your failures are too great.
If your past is too dark.
If your shame is too heavy.
If your story is too broken.
The cross answers every one of those fears.
Jesus entered the deepest darkness imaginable so that no believer would ever walk through darkness alone.
Notice something remarkable.
Psalm 22 does not end in despair.
The same Psalm Jesus quoted begins with forsakenness but ends in victory.
It moves from suffering to worship.
From agony to triumph.
From abandonment to restoration.
The final verses celebrate God's faithfulness and redemption.
Why?
Because the story was never over.
And neither is yours.
Three days after the cry of abandonment came the shout of resurrection.
The grave could not keep Him.
Death could not hold Him.
Hell could not defeat Him.
Sin could not silence Him.
The stone rolled away.
The tomb stood empty.
And history changed forever.
The resurrection proves that God's silence is never His absence.
The darkness of Friday was not the end.
Sunday was coming.
Maybe that's where you are today.
Living in the Friday of your story.
Watching dreams die.
Watching prayers remain unanswered.
Watching pain linger longer than expected.
But the Gospel reminds us that God specializes in resurrection.
He still raises dead things.
He still restores broken people.
He still redeems ruined stories.
He still transforms scandals into testimonies.
He still rewrites everything.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that good people become slightly better.
But that dead sinners are made alive through Jesus Christ.
Not that broken people repair themselves.
But that Christ restores what sin destroyed.
Not that shame wins.
But that grace triumphs.
Not that your past defines you.
But that Jesus does.
Maybe today you need to stop measuring God's love by your circumstances.
The greatest demonstration of His love was not found in an easy life.
It was found at Calvary.
At the place where the Son of God willingly endured what we deserved.
At the place where mercy flowed through wounded hands.
At the place where scandal met grace.
At the place where Heaven paid the price for rebels.
At the place where Jesus rewrote eternity.
And perhaps that is why these words remain among the most powerful ever spoken.
Because hidden inside the cry of forsakenness is the promise of redemption.
The cry that sounded like defeat became the doorway to victory.
The moment that appeared darkest became the moment salvation shined brightest.
The cross was never evidence that God had abandoned His plan.
The cross was the plan.
And because Jesus was forsaken in our place, everyone who trusts in Him can cling to this promise:
"I will never leave you nor forsake you." (Hebrews 13:5)
Never.
Not in your failure.
Not in your addiction.
Not in your grief.
Not in your depression.
Not in your doubt.
Not in your scandal.
Not in your darkest night.
If you belong to Christ, you are not abandoned.
You are pursued.
You are not forgotten.
You are remembered.
You are not beyond redemption.
You are exactly the kind of person Jesus came to save.
So if this message touched your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
You never know who is silently asking the same question Jesus quoted from Psalm 22.
What part of your story are you still trusting Jesus to redeem?
“Christ is still healing me.”
If God is still writing your testimony.
If you're ready to surrender every wound, every fear, and every secret place to Jesus Christ.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Most importantly, your support helps expand the reach of the Gospel and allows more people to encounter biblical truth, healing, hope, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the cry that sounds like abandonment is actually the beginning of resurrection.
The cross looked like the end of the story until the Author stepped out of the grave.
